::: {.why}
The static regression slope from week 12 assumes the relationship between two names is constant for ten years, which is a strong claim you have not tested and probably do not believe.
:::

## What you should be able to do tonight

- Express a time-varying hedge ratio as a state space model and say what the two variance parameters control.
- Show the dynamic hedge ratio against the rolling-window regression estimate on the same pair, and say which is smoother and why.

## Tasks <span class='task-total'>60 min</span>

::: {.task-list}
::: {.task}
<input type="checkbox" class="task-check"> [35 min]{.task-min} Implement the local level model for the hedge ratio: the state is the slope, it follows a random walk, and the observation is one log price regressed on the other. Use statsmodels statespace so the likelihood is available, and estimate the two variances by maximum likelihood rather than choosing them.
:::
::: {.task}
<input type="checkbox" class="task-check"> [25 min]{.task-min} Compare three estimates of the same hedge ratio on one plot: full-sample regression, 60-day rolling regression, and the filtered state. Then say what the ratio of the two estimated variances corresponds to, which is an effective lookback window.
:::
:::

## The running strategy

::: {.project}
The pairs strategy gains a dynamic hedge ratio estimated by maximum likelihood rather than a window length chosen by hand. The static version stays in the code as the comparison the milestone reports against.
:::

## Checkpoint

::: {.checkpoint}
Why would you use a Kalman filter for a hedge ratio rather than a rolling regression? Give an answer that is about the estimator, not about smoothness.
:::
